en: The Secret Upaniṣad of Sarasvatī
I worship that state of Rāmacandra, which is the sole object of the knowledge of Brahman free from all counter-correlates, indivisible and beyond conceptual construction.
Oṃ! May my speech be established in my mind; may my mind be established in my speech.
Be manifest before me; be the mouth of the Veda for me; do not abandon my cooked offering. By this study, I join together the days and nights.
I shall speak the Ṛta; I shall speak the Truth.
May that protect me; may it protect the speaker;
may it protect me; may it protect the speaker; may it protect the speaker.
Oṃ. Peace, peace, peace.
Hari Om.
The sages, having honored the venerable Āśvalāyana, asked him:
"By what means is that knowledge attained which illuminates the meaning of that state?
O Blessed One, tell us by the worship of what you know reality."
O best of sages, having praised and recited the *Sarasvatī-daśaślokī* together with the Ṛgvedic verses mixed with the seed-mantras, I attained supreme perfection.
The sages said:
"O observer of noble vows, tell us how the attainment of Sarasvatī occurs; by what meditation is the blessed Mahāsarasvatī pleased?"
Aśvalāyana said:
Of this great mantra, the *Śrīsarasvatī-daśaślokī*,
I, Aśvalāyana, am the seer (*ṛṣi*).
The meter is Anuṣṭubh;
the deity is Śrīvāgīśvarī;
the seed-syllable is "yadvāk".
"Devīm vācam" is the Śakti;
"Oṃ pra ṇo devī" is the Kīlaka.
The application [of the mantra] is for the sake of pleasing Him.
The ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) is performed with these: Faith, Intelligence, Wisdom, Retention, and the Goddess of Speech, Mahāsarasvatī.
Her radiance resembles frost, a pearl necklace, camphor, and the moon;
she bestows auspiciousness and is adorned with garlands of golden campaka flowers;
her limbs are enchanting, graced by lofty, full breasts like jars.
I bow to Vāṇī with my mind and speech for the sake of prosperity. || 1 ||
Oṃ. For this mantra beginning with "pra ṇo devī," Bharadvāja is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandas),
and Śrīsarasvatī is the deity (devatā).
The seed-syllable and power are by means of the *praṇava*; the pinning is [by the same];
the application is for the desired purpose;
the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is by means of the mantra.
O Sarasvatī, who in ultimate reality has as her sole nature the true essence of the meaning of the Vedānta, yet is manifested in the form of name and form— may she protect me!
Oṃ! May the goddess Sarasvatī, rich in spoils through her own riches, protect us as the guardian of inspired thoughts. 2.1.
For the mantra beginning with "ā no divaḥ," Atri is the seer (ṛṣi),
Triṣṭubh is the meter (chandas),
and Sarasvatī is the deity (devatā).
"Hrīṃ" is the seed-syllable (bīja), the power (śakti), and the pin (kīlaka).
Its application (viniyoga) is for the desired purpose. The ritual placement (nyāsa) is performed with the mantra.
May that Sarasvatī, the non-dual power of Brahman who is proclaimed as one alone throughout the four Vedas along with their limbs and sub-limbs, protect me.
Hrīṃ! May Sarasvatī, the worshipful goddess, come from the great heaven and from the mountain to our sacrifice.
May she, the butter-dripping one, who delights in our invocation, graciously hear our effective speech with favor. 2.2.
For the mantra beginning with "pāvakā naḥ," Madhucchandas is the seer (ṛṣi) and Gāyatrī is the meter (chandaḥ).
Sarasvatī is the deity; "Śrī" is the seed-syllable, the power, and the pin; its application is for the attainment of one's desired goal.
The ritual placement is performed with the mantra.
May that Sarasvatī, who exists as the very nature of phonemes, words, and sentence-meanings, and who is without beginning or end and infinite, protect me.
May the auspicious Sarasvatī, the purifier, rich in strength through her powers, desire our sacrifice with her wisdom as a source of wealth. 2.3.
For the mantra beginning with "codayitrī," Madhucchandas is the seer (ṛṣi),
Gāyatrī is the meter (chandaḥ),
and Sarasvatī is the deity (devatā).
"Blūm" is the seed-syllable power; "kīlaka" is the pinning.
The ritual placement (nyāsa) is performed with the mantra.
May that Sarasvatī protect me— she who, as the perfect sovereign of the gods, both internally and with respect to the divine, dwells facing inward as they speak.
Blūṃ! Sarasvatī, the inspirer of true words, awakening noble thoughts, has established the sacrifice. 2.4.
Of the mantra beginning with "maho arṇaḥ," Madhucchandas is the seer (ṛṣi) and Gāyatrī is the meter (chandaḥ).
Sarasvatī is the deity;
"sauri" is the seed-syllable and the power; the pin (kīlaka) is [the same];
the ritual placement (nyāsa) is performed with the mantra.

May that Sarasvatī protect me—she who, as the inner controller (antaryāmin), governs the entire universe and the three worlds; she who exists in the forms of Rudra, the Ādityas, and others; and into whom all things are again dissolved, while they meditate upon her as the one whose nature is every form.
Sauḥ! Sarasvatī, the great ocean, awakens us with her signal;
she illumines all our thoughts. 2.5.
Regarding the mantra beginning with "catvāri vāk": Dīrghatamas, the son of Ucathya, is the seer (ṛṣi);
Triṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ);
Sarasvatī is the deity (devatā).
"Aim" is the seed-syllable (bīja), the power (śakti), and the pin (kīlaka).
The ritual placement (nyāsa) is performed with the mantra.
That [Reality] which is experienced as being manifested by individual souls (jīva) through inward-turned vision;
May that Sarasvatī, who is all-pervading and whose single form is pure consciousness, protect me.
Aiṃ! Speech is measured in four quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them.
Three, hidden in the cave, do not stir; the fourth quarter of speech, humans speak. 2.6.
Regarding the mantra "yadvāgvadanti," Bhārgava is the seer (ṛṣi),
Triṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ),
and Sarasvatī is the deity (devatā).
*Klīm* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), the power (*śakti*), and the pin (*kīlaka*). The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is performed with the mantra.
That [power] which is conceptualized in eight ways through distinctions such as name, genus, and so forth—
May that Sarasvatī, manifested through her non-conceptual nature, protect me.
Klīṃ! That which the speechless ones declare as speech, the delightful Goddess of the Gods has sat down;
she has yielded the fourfold strength and the milks. Where indeed has her highest part gone? 2.7.
For the mantra "devīṃ vācam," Bhārgava is the seer (ṛṣi),
Triṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ),
and Sarasvatī is the deity (devatā).
*Sauḥ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *Śakti* is the pin (*kīlaka*). The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is performed with the mantra.
She whom all the Vedas and others, with both manifest and unmanifest voices, proclaim—
May that Sarasvatī, the cow who milks all desires, protect me.
Sauḥ! The gods generated the goddess Vāc; she, assuming all forms, is spoken by animals.
May she, the cow Vāc, yielding us joy, refreshment, and nourishment, come to us well-praised. 2.8.
For the mantra beginning with "uta tvā," Bṛhaspati is the seer (ṛṣi),
Triṣṭubh is the meter (chandas),
and Sarasvatī is the deity (devatā).

The seed-power (*bīja-śakti*) is *samit*, and the pin (*kīlaka*) is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) performed with the mantra. Having understood which [power], one destroys all bondage by means of the entire path.
The yogi goes to the supreme abode; may that Sarasvatī protect me.
One, though seeing, has not perceived Speech; another, though hearing, does not hear her.
Yet to another she has revealed her body, like a longing, well-adorned wife to her husband. (2.9)
For the mantra beginning with "ambitame," Gṛtsamada is the seer (ṛṣi),
Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ),
and Sarasvatī is the deity (devatā).
"Aim" is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), the power (*śakti*), and the pin (*kīlaka*).
The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is performed with the mantra.
Having dissolved everything consisting of name and form into that [syllable], one [proceeds] again.
May that Sarasvatī, who meditates with one-pointed focus on the form of Brahman, protect me.
Aiṃ! O most motherly, most river-like, most divine Sarasvatī!
We are as if unworthy of praise; O Mother, grant us renown. 2.10.
May Sarasvatī, who is entirely pure, who is like a female swan in the forest of lotus-faces of the four-faced one, and who is white in every way, delight eternally in my mind. 3.1.
Salutations to you, O Goddess Śāradā, dweller in the city of Kāśmīra;
I pray to you constantly—grant me the gift of knowledge. || 2 ||
Holding a rosary and a goad, bearing a noose and a book, and adorned with a necklace of pearls—may she always abide in my speech. (3)
May the goddess Mahāsarasvatī, with her conch-like neck and beautiful red lips, adorned with all ornaments, take her seat upon the tip of my tongue. (4)

She who is faith, retention, and intelligence; the goddess of speech, beloved by the Creator; she who dwells upon the tips of the tongues of her devotees; and she who bestows virtues such as tranquility.
I bow to Bhavānī, whose tresses are adorned with the crescent moon,
and who is a river of nectar that extinguishes the fever of worldly existence.
He who desires fearlessness in poetic composition, as well as devotion and liberation,
should daily praise Sarasvatī by means of this ten-verse hymn.
For him who thus constantly praises and worships Sarasvatī,
being endowed with devotion and faith, realization shall arise within six months.
Then speech proceeds spontaneously with graceful syllables, consisting of words in both prose and verse, immeasurable and intended [by the speaker]. (9)
"A text is understood even if not heard; for the most part, the poet is one who possesses the grace of Sarasvatī.
Thus, O Brahmins, did Sarasvatī herself declare this certainty.
The eternal science of the Self has been obtained by me from Brahmā himself;
my state of Brahmanhood is forever constant, by virtue of being of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss. (11)
From that, the state of primordial nature (prakṛti) was produced through the equilibrium of the qualities such as sattva;
therein, reality shines forth as the reflection of consciousness, like a reflection in a mirror.
Furthermore, through that reflection in consciousness, she appears again as threefold;
moreover, by being delimited by primordial nature (prakṛti), those two appear as the state of the Puruṣa.
For the Unborn (Aja) is indeed reflected in Māyā, which is dominated by pure Sattva;
thus it is established that Māyā is Prakṛti dominated by Sattva.
For that illusion is indeed an adventitious adjunct under His own control; moreover, for the omniscient Lord, there is mastery, unity, and omniscience. (3.15)
Because they are composed of sattva, because they are the cosmic totality (samaṣṭi), and because they are the witnesses even of the worlds,
they are able to create the world, not to create it, or to create it otherwise.
He who is called the Lord by virtue of qualities such as omniscience possesses,
through Māyā, a twofold power consisting of projection and concealment.
The power of projection (vikṣepa-śakti) creates the universe, from the subtle body (liṅga) up to the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa),
as well as the internal distinction between the seer and the seen, and externally, the distinction between Brahman and the creation.
The other power is that which veils; it is the cause of saṃsāra. It appears before the Witness, conjoined with the subtle body (liṅgadeha). || 19 ||
Through the penetration of the reflection of consciousness, there arises the empirical living being (jīva).
Its status as a living being appears even in the Witness (sākṣin) due to superimposition. (3.20)
But when that concealment has perished and difference has become manifest, it (the world) departs;
likewise, it remains having concealed the difference between the creation and Brahman.
That power by virtue of which Brahman appears as something modified—here too, through the destruction of the veil, both Brahman and the creation shine forth [in their true nature]. (22)
The difference between those two would be a modification during creation, but never in Brahman.
"It exists," "it shines," "it is dear," "form," and "name"—this is the pentad of aspects. (23)
The first triad is the form of Brahman; thereafter, the [other] two are the form of the world.
With regard to these two, name and form, he is intent upon existence, consciousness, and bliss.
One should always practice samādhi, either within the heart or externally.
Samādhi in the heart is of two kinds: with conceptualization (savikalpa) and without conceptualization (nirvikalpa). (3.25)
Furthermore, that conceptual construction (vikalpa) is twofold according to the distinction between the visible object and sound.
The visible objects, such as desire and the rest, reside in the mind; consciousness is the witness of those [objects]. (26)
This meditation, permeated by the visible object, is *samādhi* with conceptualization (*savikalpaka*).
It is unattached, being existence-consciousness-bliss (*saccidānanda*), self-luminous, and devoid of duality. (27)
This samādhi, pierced by the notion "I am," is conceptual (savikalpaka),
because it depends upon visible objects, sounds, and so forth, due to the immersion in the flavor of one's own experience.
Non-conceptual meditative absorption (samādhi) is like a lamp placed in a windless spot; it remains so whether directed toward the heart, the external world, or upon any object whatsoever. (29)
Samādhi is the separation of name and form from the initial pure state alone;
the third [type] is considered, as before, to be a state of rigidity resulting from the tasting of flavor (rasa). (3.30)
One should spend one's time continuously with these six meditative absorptions.
When identification with the body has dissolved and the Supreme Self is realized,
wherever the mind goes, there is the supreme nectar.
The knot of the heart is broken, all doubts are severed,
and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen.
"The state of being a living soul and the state of being a Lord are merely imagined in me; in reality, they do not exist.
He who understands this is liberated; of this there is no doubt. (33)
Oṃ! May my speech be established in my mind;
may my mind be established in my speech. Be manifest and clear to me.
Be the two axle-pins of my Veda; do not let the cooked [oblation] of mine be lost.
By this studied [Veda], I join together the days and nights.
I shall speak the Ṛta;
I shall speak the Truth.
May that protect me.
May it protect its speaker;
may it protect me; may it protect the speaker; may it protect the speaker.
Thus ends the Sarasvatīrahasya Upaniṣad.
